column9: Which elements are in sodium hydroxide, NaOH?
column28: Na is sodium, O is oxygen, and H is hydrogen. A new element starts at every capital letter, so Na is one symbol (not N for nitrogen) and O and H are separate.
column29: A new element symbol starts at every capital letter. A lowercase letter belongs to the capital before it.

column9: Ammonia is NH₃. How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of ammonia?
column28: The subscript 3 follows H, so there are 3 hydrogen atoms (and 1 nitrogen atom).
column29: The small number below applies only to the symbol it follows.

column9: How many chlorine atoms are in one molecule of CCl₄?
column28: The subscript 4 follows Cl, so there are 4 chlorine atoms. C has no subscript, so there is 1 carbon atom.
column29: Find the symbol Cl and look at the small number right after it.

column9: How many total atoms are in one formula unit of calcium chloride, CaCl₂?
column28: Ca: 1 (no subscript means 1). Cl: 2. Total = 1 + 2 = 3 atoms.
column29: Count each element first (no subscript means 1), then add the counts.

column9: Each symbol in a chemical formula, such as Na or Cl, stands for one ___.
column28: Each symbol stands for one element. For example, NaCl contains the elements sodium (Na) and chlorine (Cl).
column29: What do you find in each box of the periodic table?

column9: A substance made of two or more elements chemically combined, like NaCl or CO₂, is called a ___.
column28: A compound is two or more elements chemically combined. NaCl (sodium + chlorine) and CO₂ (carbon + oxygen) are both compounds.
column29: It is not an element and not a mixture. Starts with c.

column9: Match each term to its meaning.
column14: Subscript :: Small number that applies only to the symbol it follows
column15: Coefficient :: Big number in front that multiplies everything in the formula
column16: Molecule :: Unit made of nonmetal atoms that share electrons (covalently bonded)
column17: Formula unit :: Smallest repeating unit of an ionic substance like NaCl
column28: A subscript (small, below) counts only the symbol before it. A coefficient (big, in front) multiplies the whole formula. A molecule is covalently bonded; a formula unit is the repeating unit of an ionic compound.
column29: Think about where each number sits: small and below, or big and in front?

column9: In H₂O, the subscript 2 applies to both the hydrogen and the oxygen.
column28: False. A subscript applies only to the symbol it follows. H₂O has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.
column29: Which symbol does the small 2 come right after?

column9: CO₂ contains one carbon atom, even though no 1 is written after the C.
column28: True. When a symbol has no subscript, there is 1 atom of that element. CO₂ has 1 carbon atom and 2 oxygen atoms.
column29: What does it mean when a symbol has no small number after it?

column9: In sodium sulfate, Na₂SO₄, what does the 4 tell you?
column28: The subscript 4 comes right after O, so it means 4 oxygen atoms. It does not touch Na or S, and it is not a coefficient, so it does not count formula units.
column29: A subscript applies only to the symbol it follows. Which symbol is right before the 4?

column9: How many different elements are in potassium permanganate, KMnO₄?
column28: K (potassium), Mn (manganese), and O (oxygen): 3 different elements. Mn is one symbol because the lowercase n belongs to the capital M.
column29: Count the capital letters. Each capital letter starts a new element symbol.

column9: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆. How many hydrogen atoms are in one molecule of glucose?
column28: The subscript right after H is 12, so there are 12 hydrogen atoms. (There are also 6 C and 6 O.)
column29: Find H and read the whole number right after it, even if it has two digits.

column9: Which of these includes a coefficient?
column28: A coefficient is the big number written in front of the whole formula. Only 2NH₃ has one. The other numbers are all subscripts.
column29: Look for a full-size number at the very front, not a small number below a symbol.

column9: Which elements are in calcium nitrate, Ca(NO₃)₂? Select all that apply.
column28: Ca = calcium, N = nitrogen, O = oxygen. Carbon (C) is not there because the lowercase a makes Ca one symbol; sodium is Na, which is not in the formula.
column29: Split the formula at every capital letter. Ca is one symbol, not C plus a.

column9: Iron(III) oxide (rust) is Fe₂O₃. How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit?
column28: The subscript after O is 3, so there are 3 oxygen atoms (and 2 iron atoms).
column29: Which number comes right after the O?

column9: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of Ca(NO₃)₂?
column28: The outside 2 multiplies everything inside the parentheses: O = 3 × 2 = 6. A common mistake is counting only the 3 inside.
column29: Draw an arrow from the outside subscript to every atom inside the parentheses.

column9: Ammonium nitrate is NH₄NO₃. How many total atoms are in one formula unit?
column28: N appears twice: 1 + 1 = 2. H = 4. O = 3. Total = 2 + 4 + 3 = 9 atoms.
column29: N shows up in two places. Count every symbol with its subscript, then add.

column9: How many total atoms are in one formula unit of KMnO₄?
column28: K = 1, Mn = 1, O = 4. Total = 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 atoms.
column29: Mn is one atom of manganese, not two atoms. Then add each count.

column9: How many hydrogen atoms are in one formula unit of aluminum hydroxide, Al(OH)₃?
column28: The outside 3 multiplies everything in (OH): H = 1 × 3 = 3 (and O = 3).
column29: H has no subscript inside the parentheses, so it starts at 1. What does the outside number do to it?

column9: How many total atoms are in one formula unit of Na₂SO₄?
column28: Na = 2, S = 1, O = 4. Total = 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 atoms.
column29: Count each element (no subscript means 1), then add.

column9: How many oxygen atoms are shown in 3H₂SO₄?
column28: Each H₂SO₄ has 4 O. The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 4 × 3 = 12 oxygen atoms.
column29: The big number in front multiplies everything. Find O in one unit first.

column9: How many total atoms are shown in 3CCl₄?
column28: One CCl₄ has 1 + 4 = 5 atoms. The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 5 × 3 = 15 atoms.
column29: Find the total atoms in one molecule first, then multiply by the big number in front.

column9: In 4H₂O, what is the difference between the 4 and the 2?
column14: The 4 is a subscript for every atom; the 2 is a coefficient for H
column15: The 4 and the 2 are added, so there are 6 hydrogen atoms
column16: The 4 counts oxygen atoms; the 2 counts hydrogen atoms
column17: The 4 multiplies the whole formula; the 2 applies only to H
column28: The 4 is a coefficient: it multiplies everything (4 water molecules). The 2 is a subscript: it applies only to H. So 4H₂O has 8 H and 4 O. Never add them (4 + 2 = 6 is a common mistake).
column29: Big number in front vs. small number below: which one touches everything?

column9: In Ca(NO₃)₂, which atoms does the 2 outside the parentheses multiply?
column16: The calcium, nitrogen, and oxygen atoms
column28: An outside subscript multiplies every atom inside the parentheses: N and O. Ca is outside the parentheses, so it stays at 1.
column29: Draw an arrow from the outside 2 to every atom inside the parentheses. Is Ca inside?

column9: Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂, contains 1 oxygen atom and 2 hydrogen atoms.
column28: False. The outside 2 multiplies both O and H inside the parentheses: 2 O and 2 H. Saying 1 O and 2 H applies the 2 only to H.
column29: Which atoms are inside the parentheses with the outside 2?

column9: A formula with more atoms always has more mass than a formula with fewer atoms.
column28: False. Atoms of different elements have different masses. NH₃ has 4 atoms and CO₂ has only 3, but CO₂ is heavier because carbon and oxygen atoms are much heavier than hydrogen atoms.
column29: Is a hydrogen atom as heavy as an oxygen atom? Check the atomic masses on the periodic table.

column9: Which formulas contain exactly 4 oxygen atoms? Select all that apply.
column28: Na₂SO₄: 4. KMnO₄: 4. Ca(NO₃)₂: 3 × 2 = 6. Al(OH)₃: 1 × 3 = 3. CO₂: 2. 2CO₂: 2 × 2 = 4.
column29: Check each one: the outside subscript multiplies what is inside parentheses, and a coefficient multiplies everything.

column9: Put the steps for counting the atoms in a formula like 2Al(OH)₃ in order.
column14: Multiply each one-unit count by the coefficient in front
column15: List each element symbol in the formula
column16: Add the counts to get the total atoms
column17: Count the atoms of each element in ONE formula unit, using the outside subscript on everything inside the parentheses
column28: List the elements, use the outside subscript on everything inside the parentheses, multiply every count by the coefficient, then add for the total.
column29: You need to know which elements are there before you count them, and you add up only at the very end.

column9: Match each formula to the total number of atoms in one unit.
column29: Add the atoms of each element. Remember the outside 2 multiplies everything in (NO₃).

column9: Ammonium sulfate is (NH₄)₂SO₄. How many hydrogen atoms are in one formula unit?
column28: The outside 2 multiplies everything in (NH₄): H = 4 × 2 = 8.
column29: Draw an arrow from the outside 2 to each atom inside the parentheses.

column9: How many oxygen atoms are in one formula unit of magnesium phosphate, Mg₃(PO₄)₂?
column28: The outside 2 multiplies everything in (PO₄): O = 4 × 2 = 8. The Mg₃ subscript belongs only to Mg.
column29: Which subscript is outside the parentheses with the oxygen? The 3 after Mg does not touch O.

column9: Sodium acetate is NaC₂H₃O₂. How many total atoms are in one formula unit?
column29: Go symbol by symbol (capital letters) and write each count, then add.

column9: Which formula has the most atoms in one unit?
column28: K₂O: 3. SiO₂: 3. Li₃N: 3 + 1 = 4. NO: 2. Li₃N has the most.
column29: Find the total atoms in each one (no subscript means 1), then compare.

column9: Which formulas are made of exactly 3 different elements? Select all that apply.
column28: LiOH: Li, O, H (3). NH₄NO₃: N, H, O (3; N appears twice but is one element). K₂CO₃: K, C, O (3). CO₂, MgCl₂, and H₂O₂ each have only 2 elements.
column29: Count different symbols, not atoms. If a symbol shows up twice, it is still one element.

column9: How many hydrogen atoms are shown in 5H₂O?
column28: Each H₂O has 2 H. The coefficient 5 multiplies everything: 2 × 5 = 10 hydrogen atoms.
column29: The big number in front multiplies everything. Multiply, don't add.

column9: Ammonium phosphate is (NH₄)₃PO₄. How many total atoms are in one formula unit?
column28: N = 1 × 3 = 3, H = 4 × 3 = 12, P = 1, O = 4. Total = 3 + 12 + 1 + 4 = 20 atoms. The outside 3 does not touch PO₄.
column29: Use the outside 3 on N and H only, then count the P and O after the parentheses.

column9: How many oxygen atoms are shown in 2Al₂(SO₄)₃?
column28: In one Al₂(SO₄)₃: O = 4 × 3 = 12. The coefficient 2 doubles everything: 12 × 2 = 24 oxygen atoms.
column29: Work inside out: outside subscript first, then the coefficient in front.

column9: How many total atoms are shown in 3Ca(NO₃)₂?
column28: One Ca(NO₃)₂: Ca 1, N 1 × 2 = 2, O 3 × 2 = 6, total 9. The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 9 × 3 = 27 atoms.
column29: Find the total for one unit first (use the outside subscript), then multiply by the coefficient.

column9: How many hydrogen atoms are shown in 4(NH₄)₂SO₄?
column28: One (NH₄)₂SO₄ has H = 4 × 2 = 8. The coefficient 4 multiplies everything: 8 × 4 = 32 hydrogen atoms.
column29: Multiply the inside subscript by the outside subscript, then by the big number in front.

column9: How many total atoms are shown in 3Mg₃(PO₄)₂?
column28: One Mg₃(PO₄)₂: Mg 3, P 1 × 2 = 2, O 4 × 2 = 8, total 13. The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 13 × 3 = 39 atoms.
column29: Count one formula unit first (the outside 2 only touches P and O), then multiply by the coefficient.

column9: How many nitrogen atoms are shown in 3Fe(NO₃)₂?
column28: One Fe(NO₃)₂ has N = 1 × 2 = 2. The coefficient 3 multiplies everything: 2 × 3 = 6 nitrogen atoms.
column29: N has no subscript inside the parentheses, so start at 1. Then use the outside subscript and the coefficient.

column9: Three students count the oxygen atoms in Fe₂(SO₄)₃. Ana said 4. Ben said 7. Cal said 12. Who is right, and what did the other two do?
column14: Ana is right; Ben added 4 + 3, and Cal multiplied when he should not have
column15: Cal is right; Ana ignored the outside 3, and Ben added 4 + 3 instead of multiplying
column16: Ben is right; Ana ignored the outside 3, and Cal multiplied 4 × 3 by mistake
column17: Cal is right; Ana added 4 + 3, and Ben ignored the outside 3
column28: O = 4 inside × 3 outside = 12, so Cal is right. Ana counted only inside the parentheses (4) and ignored the outside 3. Ben added 4 + 3 = 7 instead of multiplying.
column29: Find the correct count first (inside subscript × outside subscript), then figure out how someone could get 4 and how someone could get 7.

column9: Dev counted 4Na₂CO₃ as Na 8, C 1, O 3. What mistake did he make?
column14: He used the coefficient only on the first element instead of on everything
column15: He added the coefficient to each subscript instead of multiplying
column16: He used the subscript 2 on every element in the formula
column17: He counted correctly; a coefficient only applies to the first element
column28: The coefficient 4 multiplies everything, so 4Na₂CO₃ has Na 2 × 4 = 8, C 1 × 4 = 4, and O 3 × 4 = 12. Dev multiplied only Na.
column29: Which counts did Dev multiply by 4, and which did he leave alone?

column9: Eli says one formula unit of (NH₄)₂SO₄ has 10 atoms. Check his count. What is the correct total number of atoms?
column28: N = 1 × 2 = 2, H = 4 × 2 = 8, S = 1, O = 4. Total = 2 + 8 + 1 + 4 = 15. Eli got 10 (1 + 4 + 1 + 4) because he ignored the outside 2.
column29: Did Eli use the 2 outside the parentheses? Recount N and H with it.

column9: Maya notices that H₂O and CO₂ both have 3 atoms per molecule. She says they must be the same substance. Is she right?
column14: Yes, because the same number of atoms makes the same substance
column15: Yes, because both formulas have a subscript of 2
column16: No, because they are made of different elements in different combinations
column17: No, because H₂O has more total atoms than CO₂
column28: A formula tells which elements and how many of each. H₂O is 2 H + 1 O; CO₂ is 1 C + 2 O. Different elements make different substances, even with the same total of 3 atoms.
column29: Look at which elements are in each formula, not just how many atoms.

column9: A compound has 2 aluminum atoms, 3 carbon atoms, and 9 oxygen atoms in one formula unit. Which formula matches?
column28: Al₂(CO₃)₃: Al 2, C 1 × 3 = 3, O 3 × 3 = 9. Al₂CO₃ has only 1 C and 3 O; Al₃(CO₃)₂ has 3 Al; Al(CO₃)₃ has 1 Al.
column29: Count Al, C, and O in each choice, using the outside subscript on everything inside the parentheses.

column9: Which shows a total of 2 iron atoms, 6 nitrogen atoms, and 18 oxygen atoms?
column28: 2Fe(NO₃)₃: Fe 1 × 2 = 2, N 1 × 3 × 2 = 6, O 3 × 3 × 2 = 18. Fe₂(NO₃)₃ has 3 N and 9 O; 2Fe(NO₃)₂ has 4 N and 12 O; Fe(NO₃)₆ has only 1 Fe.
column29: For each choice, count one unit with the outside subscript, then apply the coefficient if there is one.

column9: Which of these show exactly 12 oxygen atoms? Select all that apply.
column28: Al₂(SO₄)₃: 4 × 3 = 12. 6CO₂: 2 × 6 = 12. Ca(NO₃)₂: 3 × 2 = 6. 3KMnO₄: 4 × 3 = 12. (NH₄)₂SO₄: 4 (the outside 2 is not on SO₄). 2Al(OH)₃: 1 × 3 × 2 = 6.
column29: For each, multiply inside subscript × outside subscript × coefficient, but only for the oxygen atoms actually inside those parentheses.

column9: How many more hydrogen atoms are shown in 2(NH₄)₂SO₄ than in 3Al(OH)₃?
column28: 2(NH₄)₂SO₄: H = 4 × 2 × 2 = 16. 3Al(OH)₃: H = 1 × 3 × 3 = 9. Difference = 16 − 9 = 7 more hydrogen atoms.
column29: Count the hydrogen in each one separately (inside × outside × coefficient), then subtract.

column9: Put these formulas in order from fewest to most total atoms in one unit.
column28: Al(OH)₃: 7. Ca(NO₃)₂: 9. (NH₄)₂SO₄: 15. Al₂(SO₄)₃: 17. (NH₄)₃PO₄: 20.
column29: Find the total for each formula on scratch paper first, using the outside subscripts, then sort.
